{"summary":"The design automates the refund workflow from Zendesk request through Shopify/3PL verification, a finance approval checkpoint, and Stripe issuance, but it cannot reconcile the stated 60-second refund promise with the stated hard finance approval control and the fixed daily 3PL CSV / 4pm batch cadence — these are structural conflicts in the input, not automation choices, and the design surfaces them rather than silently picking a winner.","data_flow_description":"A refund request enters via a Zendesk ticket and is normalised into a refund record. That record is checked against Shopify order data and the daily 3PL CSV to determine whether the warehouse has confirmed the return; requests without confirmation wait for the next daily CSV. Confirmed requests are queued for the finance team's fixed 4pm daily batch review, since the auditor control requires approval before money moves. Approved refunds are sent to Stripe for issuance, and the resulting outcome (approved/refunded or rejected) is written back to Zendesk to notify the customer. Nothing in this flow can complete within 60 seconds once either the CSV wait or the 4pm batch is in the path.","components":[{"name":"Refund Request Intake","responsibility":"Capture and normalise refund requests as they arrive from support conversations.","inputs":"Zendesk ticket/webhook data for a refund request","outputs":"A normalised refund request record (order reference, customer, requested amount)","failure_handling":"If the Zendesk webhook fails or data is incomplete, the request is logged as unprocessed and not passed downstream until retried.","external_system":"Zendesk","integration_direction":"inbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[7]},{"name":"Order & Return Verification","responsibility":"Confirm the refund request against Shopify order data and the 3PL's daily warehouse-return CSV before it can proceed to approval.","inputs":"Normalised refund request, Shopify order record, daily 3PL CSV","outputs":"A verification status: warehouse-confirmed and eligible, or pending (no confirmation yet)","failure_handling":"If the 3PL CSV for the day has not yet been received or does not contain a matching confirmation, the request is held in a pending state until the next daily CSV arrives; it does not advance to approval.","external_system":"Shopify, 3PL (CSV feed)","integration_direction":"inbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[5,8,9]},{"name":"Finance Approval Queue","responsibility":"Present warehouse-confirmed refund requests to the finance team for the mandatory approval control, batched to the fixed daily review time.","inputs":"Verified (warehouse-confirmed) refund requests, awaiting finance decision","outputs":"An approved-or-rejected decision per refund, produced once per day at 4pm","failure_handling":"If the 4pm review is missed or delayed, requests remain queued and unapproved rather than being auto-approved or auto-issued, since approval is a hard control.","external_system":null,"integration_direction":null,"grounded_in_context_indices":[1,3,4]},{"name":"Refund Issuance","responsibility":"Execute the Stripe refund for requests that have received finance approval.","inputs":"Approved refund records with amount and order reference","outputs":"A Stripe refund transaction and its confirmation or failure result","failure_handling":"If the Stripe API call fails, the refund is not marked complete and is flagged for retry or manual reconciliation rather than silently dropped.","external_system":"Stripe","integration_direction":"outbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[6]},{"name":"Customer Notification","responsibility":"Inform the customer, via the support channel, of the outcome of their refund request.","inputs":"Refund outcome (issued, rejected, or still pending) per request","outputs":"A Zendesk update or reply to the customer's ticket","failure_handling":"If the notification cannot be posted back to Zendesk, the refund outcome is still recorded internally and the notification is retried rather than the refund being reversed.","external_system":"Zendesk","integration_direction":"outbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[0,7]}],"unknown_disposition":[{"context_index":11,"disposition":"assumed","statement":"The design assumes finance approval is the one permitted human checkpoint in an otherwise automated flow, because the input describes it as a 'hard auditor control' which outweighs the general no-human-involvement goal; this is an assumption, not a stated resolution, and should be confirmed."},{"context_index":12,"disposition":"deferred","statement":"The design applies the same verification-then-approval path uniformly to all refund amounts rather than fast-tracking low-value refunds; if a value threshold for expedited handling is confirmed, the Finance Approval Queue and its cadence would need to split into a fast path and a batched path."},{"context_index":13,"disposition":"excluded","statement":"The design treats the daily 3PL CSV as the fixed confirmation mechanism and does not build a real-time warehouse confirmation integration; if the 3PL can provide a faster signal (webhook/API), the Order & Return Verification component would need to be redesigned around it to reduce the daily-cadence bottleneck."}],"trade_offs":[],"rejected_approaches":[]}

{"factors":[{"factor":"workflow","score":3,"justification":"The flow has a linear backbone (intake → verification → approval → issuance → notification) but includes a wait-state branch for unconfirmed warehouse returns and a batch gate at finance approval, giving it moderate conditionality rather than a pure straight-through sequence."},{"factor":"integration","score":3,"justification":"Three external systems are involved — Zendesk (inbound/outbound), Shopify, and Stripe — plus a file-based 3PL CSV feed, all with conventional, well-documented interfaces except the CSV which is a lower-fidelity batch mechanism; this is several systems of moderate heterogeneity, not many or unstable ones."},{"factor":"data_logic","score":2,"justification":"The transformations are largely reconciliation checks (matching refund request to Shopify order and to CSV return confirmation) and status propagation, with no extensive reshaping or dense rule sets described beyond confirmation matching and approval gating."},{"factor":"failure_risk","score":4,"justification":"The design carries real consequence — money movement via Stripe under a hard auditor control, combined with two irreconcilable cadence constraints (60-second promise vs. daily CSV and 4pm batch) that the architecture explicitly surfaces rather than resolves; failure to hold state correctly across the pending/approval/issuance stages risks either bypassing the auditor control or violating the SLA, demanding careful ordering and non-silent handling at each stage."},{"factor":"operational","score":3,"justification":"Running the daily 3PL CSV ingestion and the fixed 4pm finance batch requires periodic attention (monitoring for missed CSVs, unapproved queues, and Stripe failures flagged for manual reconciliation), representing routine oversight rather than a fully unattended or a constantly monitored system."}]}

{"phases":[{"ordinal":1,"name":"Intake and normalisation","objective":"Build the entry point that captures refund requests from Zendesk and normalises them into a working record, establishing the data every downstream component consumes.","components":["Refund Request Intake"],"depends_on":[],"outcome":"A refund request raised in Zendesk is captured and converted into a normalised internal record; nothing downstream exists yet, so no refund actually progresses further.","estimate":null},{"ordinal":2,"name":"Order and return verification against the daily CSV","objective":"Build the check against Shopify order data and the 3PL's daily CSV that determines whether a warehouse return has been confirmed, resolving the mechanism for context index 9's dependency and applying the exclusion disposition for index 13 (no real-time confirmation is built).","components":["Order & Return Verification"],"depends_on":[1],"outcome":"An intake refund record can be automatically checked against Shopify and the day's 3PL CSV; confirmed requests are marked eligible, unconfirmed ones held pending until the next CSV. No refund can yet be approved or issued.","estimate":null},{"ordinal":3,"name":"Finance approval checkpoint","objective":"Build the batched approval queue that implements the hard auditor control (context index 1), applying the assumed disposition for index 11 that finance approval is the sole permitted human checkpoint, and fixing it to the stated 4pm daily cadence (index 3) — this is the component that structurally conflicts with the 60-second promise (index 2), so it is proven here rather than deferred, since it is the riskiest and most rigid dependency in the flow.","components":["Finance Approval Queue"],"depends_on":[2],"outcome":"Verified refund requests reach a daily 4pm batch review where finance can approve or reject them; no refund can move to issuance without this step, and the pending/rejected states are visible to whoever operates the queue.","estimate":null},{"ordinal":4,"name":"Refund issuance","objective":"Build the Stripe integration that executes approved refunds, consuming the Finance Approval Queue's output.","components":["Refund Issuance"],"depends_on":[3],"outcome":"An approved refund record is automatically sent to Stripe and issued or flagged for retry on failure; money can now leave the account, but only for refunds that passed verification and approval.","estimate":null},{"ordinal":5,"name":"Customer notification and closed loop","objective":"Build the outcome write-back to Zendesk so the customer is informed of the result, completing the end-to-end flow described in the architecture's data flow.","components":["Customer Notification"],"depends_on":[4],"outcome":"The full designed flow runs end to end: a Zendesk refund request is normalised, checked against Shopify/3PL CSV, queued for the fixed daily finance review, issued via Stripe on approval, and the customer is notified of the outcome — with the unresolved structural conflict between the 60-second promise (index 2) and the daily CSV/4pm batch cadence (index 10) still standing and visible to the business, since no phase can build around it without further input.","estimate":null}],"sequencing_rationale":"The order follows what each component consumes: verification needs a normalised request from Intake, approval needs a warehouse-confirmed request from Verification, issuance needs an approved record from the Finance Approval Queue, and notification needs an issuance outcome. The Finance Approval Queue is built as its own phase, isolated from a later 'hardening' step, because it is where the input's stated hard auditor control (index 1) and fixed 4pm cadence (index 3) live, and because it is the component most directly in tension with the 60-second promise (index 2) and the inferred cadence conflict (index 10) — proving it early surfaces that conflict rather than papering over it later. The daily-CSV dependency (index 9) is resolved inside Verification itself, per the exclusion disposition for index 13, rather than deferred to a later integration phase, since no faster signal is confirmed. The design is complete after phase 5; no phase builds nothing, and every architecture component appears exactly once in the phase that builds it."}

{"risks":[{"component":"Finance Approval Queue","description":"The stated 60-second refund promise and the fixed 4pm-once-daily finance approval batch are structurally incompatible; every refund routed through this queue will breach the 60-second SLA regardless of implementation, since approval only happens once per day.","severity":5,"likelihood":5,"mitigation":"Escalate the conflict to the business before building: confirm whether the 60-second promise, the daily batch, or the hard finance-approval control must give way, since the design cannot satisfy all three as stated."},{"component":"Order & Return Verification","description":"The daily 3PL CSV is the only warehouse-confirmation signal, so any refund request that arrives after that day's CSV has been processed must wait roughly 24 hours before it can even reach the finance queue, compounding the SLA breach and making the delay routine rather than occasional given 200 refunds/week arriving continuously.","severity":4,"likelihood":5,"mitigation":"Confirm with the 3PL whether a faster (webhook/API) confirmation is available (context index 13 was excluded from this design); if not, set customer-facing expectations that refunds cannot be near-instant while this dependency stands."},{"component":"Refund Request Intake","description":"The design assumes finance approval is the one permitted human checkpoint (context index 11, disposed as 'assumed'); if the auditor's 'no human involvement' requirement is intended to exclude even the finance step, the entire architecture's approval stage is non-compliant and would need rebuilding around a different control.","severity":4,"likelihood":3,"mitigation":"Obtain explicit confirmation from the auditor/compliance owner on whether finance review is exempt from the no-human-involvement rule before implementing the Finance Approval Queue as designed."},{"component":"Refund Issuance","description":"Bulk refunds up to £2,000 pass through the same automated Stripe issuance path as the £45-average refunds with no distinct control or extra check called out for high-value cases, so a verification or approval error on a bulk refund has an outsized financial impact compared to the typical £45 case.","severity":4,"likelihood":2,"mitigation":"Add a value-based check in the Finance Approval Queue or Refund Issuance step that flags refunds above a threshold (e.g. near £2,000) for an explicit secondary confirmation or amount cross-check against the original order before the Stripe call is made."},{"component":"3PL (CSV feed)","description":"The Order & Return Verification component depends on a daily CSV from an external 3PL with no stated fallback if the file is late, malformed, or missing a given day; the failure_handling only describes holding requests pending, which silently extends the delay without alerting anyone.","severity":3,"likelihood":3,"mitigation":"Add a check that the daily CSV was received and parsed successfully by a fixed time each day, and alert an operator if it is missing or fails validation, so delays are visible rather than silent."},{"component":"Stripe","description":"If the Stripe refund call fails after finance approval, the failure_handling flags it for retry or manual reconciliation, but manual reconciliation reintroduces the human involvement the design otherwise seeks to eliminate, and there is no stated volume or frequency expectation for how often this manual path would be invoked.","severity":3,"likelihood":2,"mitigation":"Define an automated retry policy with backoff for transient Stripe failures before escalating to manual reconciliation, and cap the number of automatic retries to avoid indefinite pending states."},{"component":"Customer Notification","description":"Refund requests that are pending (awaiting the next daily CSV or the next 4pm batch) may not receive an interim status update to Zendesk, since the component's stated inputs are outcome-based (issued/rejected/pending) but failure_handling only addresses notification delivery failure, not proactive pending-status communication.","severity":2,"likelihood":4,"mitigation":"Add an interim automated Zendesk reply when a request enters a pending state (awaiting CSV or awaiting batch) so customers are not left without any communication during the multi-hour or multi-day wait."}],"no_risks_statement":null}

{"edge_cases":[{"component":"Order & Return Verification","scenario":"A refund request arrives for an order whose warehouse return confirmation is not yet present in that day's 3PL CSV, or where a return never appears in any CSV due to a mismatch (e.g. wrong order reference)","consequence":"The request is stuck in pending status indefinitely with no path to resolution, and the customer receives no refund and no explanation of the delay","handling":"Held in pending state per its stated failure_handling until the next daily CSV; but the design does not specify an escalation or timeout for requests that never match, so a stuck-request path should be added"},{"component":"Finance Approval Queue","scenario":"A refund request becomes warehouse-confirmed after the 4pm batch cutoff on a given day","consequence":"The request waits a full extra day before finance can even see it, compounding the conflict with the 60-second promise into a multi-day delay","handling":"Not addressed in failure_handling; the component's cadence design should explicitly define a cutoff time so late-arriving confirmations are queued for the next day's batch rather than left ambiguous"},{"component":"Finance Approval Queue","scenario":"Finance rejects a refund request (e.g. return not eligible) rather than approving it","consequence":"The design's data_flow describes 'approved/refunded or rejected' outcomes but the Finance Approval Queue's outputs only state 'approved-or-rejected decision' without detailing what happens operationally on rejection","handling":"Customer Notification component covers relaying a 'rejected' outcome, but Finance Approval Queue itself should record a rejection reason for audit purposes, which is not currently specified"},{"component":"Refund Issuance","scenario":"A refund for the higher end of the stated value range (up to £2,000 for bulk orders) fails at Stripe due to insufficient account balance or a Stripe-side hold","consequence":"A large refund silently fails to complete while appearing to the customer or finance as approved, breaking the auditor control's guarantee that approved refunds are issued","handling":"failure_handling flags it for retry or manual reconciliation, but does not distinguish high-value failures for priority handling despite the £2,000 volume noted in context"},{"component":"external_system: 3PL (CSV feed)","scenario":"The daily CSV from the 3PL fails to arrive at all on a given day, or arrives malformed/corrupted","consequence":"All pending refund verifications for that day stall with no confirmation source, cascading into Finance Approval Queue having nothing to review","handling":"Not addressed anywhere in the architecture; Order & Return Verification's failure_handling only covers 'not yet received or no matching confirmation', not a fully missing or malformed feed"},{"component":"Refund Request Intake","scenario":"The same refund request is submitted twice, e.g. a customer replies to the same Zendesk ticket or opens a duplicate ticket for the same order","consequence":"Two refund records could proceed through verification and approval independently, resulting in a duplicate Stripe refund for the same order","handling":"Not addressed in failure_handling, which covers only webhook failure or incomplete data, not duplicate detection"},{"component":"Finance Approval Queue","scenario":"Volume of confirmed requests on a given day approaches or exceeds the stated average of roughly 29/week concentrated into a single 4pm batch, or a backlog accumulates from a missed CSV day","consequence":"Finance may face a larger-than-typical batch to review in one sitting, increasing risk of rushed or skipped review of the hard auditor control","handling":"Not addressed; the design does not specify batch-size limits or escalation if backlog grows"}],"practices":[{"applies_to":"Refund Issuance","practice":"Idempotent Stripe refund calls keyed on the Shopify order reference or refund request ID","rationale":"Prevents a duplicate refund request (from Refund Request Intake) or a retried failed Stripe call from issuing two refunds against the same order"},{"applies_to":"Order & Return Verification","practice":"Reconciliation check between the 3PL CSV's order references and open pending requests, flagging entries that fail to match after a defined number of daily CSV cycles","rationale":"The design holds unmatched requests in pending state indefinitely; without a reconciliation step, mismatches (e.g. wrong order reference in the CSV) would never surface"},{"applies_to":"Finance Approval Queue","practice":"Record and retain the finance decision (approve/reject) with reviewer identity and timestamp for each refund","rationale":"The requirement describes this step as a 'hard auditor control', which implies the decision itself must be auditable, not just gated"}]}

{"criteria_applied":[{"criterion":"The architecture rests on two unresolved structural conflicts: the 60-second refund promise vs. the fixed 4pm daily finance batch, and the no-human-involvement rule vs. the mandatory finance approval control","context_index":2,"component":null},{"criterion":"The daily 3PL CSV and the 4pm batch both impose a once-a-day cadence that cannot be reconciled with a 60-second SLA by any platform choice","context_index":10,"component":null},{"criterion":"Volume is low (about 200 refunds/week, average £45, occasional £2,000 cases), which would ordinarily support a lightweight no-code integration if the conflicts were resolved","context_index":4,"component":null},{"criterion":"Whether finance approval is meant as the sole permitted human checkpoint, or excluded entirely from 'no human involvement,' is unresolved and materially changes what any platform would need to enforce","context_index":11,"component":"Finance Approval Queue"},{"criterion":"No context element states a budget, team size, or in-house technical capability, so no platform can be selected on cost or operability grounds","context_index":null,"component":null}],"recommended_platform":null,"also_required":[],"rationale":"The architecture itself flags that the 60-second refund promise, the hard finance-approval control, and the fixed daily cadences (4pm batch review and daily 3PL CSV) are mutually incompatible as stated — not an automation-design problem but a business-requirements conflict. Selecting a platform now would mean silently encoding one interpretation of these contradictions (e.g. dropping the 60-second promise, or dropping the human approval control, or treating the daily cadence as acceptable) without the business having decided that.
